title: The Young Doctor's First Case
summary: A girl who dreams of becoming a doctor shadows her aunt, a family physician, for a day and learns that comforting a frightened patient matters as much as medical skill.
poll: Being kind to a scared patient matters just as much as having good medical skill.

versions.title: The Young Doctor's First Case
versions.text:
Lina wants to be a doctor. Her aunt is a doctor too. Her name is Aunt Huda.

One day, Lina goes to work with her aunt. She watches and helps.

A boy comes in. His name is Omar. He fell off his bike. His foot hurts a lot. Omar is the patient. He is scared. He cries.

Aunt Huda looks at his foot. She is careful. Lina sits by Omar. She talks to him. She tells him a joke.

Omar stops crying. He feels okay now. Aunt Huda wraps his foot. She says, "Rest now. Put ice on it."

Omar smiles. He says thank you to Lina.

At the end of the day, Aunt Huda talks to Lina. She says being kind is just as good as being a smart doctor.

Lina smiles too. She wants to be a doctor even more now.

versions.title: The Young Doctor's First Case
versions.text:
Lina wants to be a doctor one day. Her aunt is already a doctor. Her name is Aunt Huda.

One Saturday, Lina goes to work with her aunt. She watches and helps all day.

A boy named Omar comes in. He fell off his bike and hurt his foot. Omar is the patient, and he is very scared. He starts to cry.

Aunt Huda looks at his sore foot. She is careful and gentle. Lina sits down next to Omar. She talks to him in a soft voice. She tells him a funny little joke.

Omar stops crying at last. He feels a bit better now. Aunt Huda wraps his foot with care. She says, "Rest your foot, and put some ice on it."

Omar smiles at last. He says thank you to kind Lina.

At the end of the long day, Aunt Huda tells Lina something. She says being kind to a scared patient matters just as much as being a good doctor.

Lina smiles back. Now she wants to be a doctor even more than before.

versions.title: The Young Doctor's First Case
versions.text:
Lina has wanted to be a doctor since she was small. Her aunt, Huda, is already a doctor. She works at a small clinic.

One Saturday, Aunt Huda lets Lina come along. Lina watches her all day. Lina is excited. She promises to be careful and quiet.

Soon, a boy named Omar comes in with his mom. Omar fell off his bike at school. Now his foot hurts a lot. He is the first patient of the day. He looks very scared. Tears run down his face.

Aunt Huda kneels down. She looks at his sore foot. She is careful not to move it too fast. Lina sits down beside Omar. She talks to him in a soft voice. She tells him a funny story about her own bike.

Slowly, Omar stops crying. He feels a little braver now. Someone is talking kindly to him. Aunt Huda wraps his foot. She tells his mom, "Let him rest, and put ice on it twice a day."

Before they leave, Omar smiles. He thanks kind Lina for helping him feel brave.

That evening, Aunt Huda tells Lina something true: being kind to a scared patient matters just as much as good doctor skills. Lina smiles. She wants to be a doctor even more now.

versions.title: The Young Doctor's First Case
versions.text:
Lina has dreamed of being a doctor since she was small. Her aunt, Huda, already works as a doctor. She works at a busy little clinic near their home. She treats whole families, from tiny babies to old grandparents.

One Saturday, Aunt Huda lets Lina come along and watch her. Lina is thrilled. She promises to stay careful and quiet while she watches.

Soon, a boy named Omar walks in with his worried mom. Omar had fallen off his bike on the way to school. Now his foot hurts badly. He is the very first patient of the morning. He looks very scared. Tears roll down his cheeks.

Aunt Huda kneels down slowly. She looks closely at his sore foot. She is careful never to move it too fast. Lina sits down right beside Omar. She talks to him in a soft voice. She tells him a funny story about the time she fell off her own bike.

Little by little, Omar stops crying. He feels a bit braver now. Someone is talking so kindly to him. Aunt Huda wraps a bandage around his foot. She tells his mom, "Let him rest, and put ice on it twice a day."

Before leaving, Omar smiles. He thanks kind Lina for helping him feel brave enough to sit still.

That evening, Aunt Huda tells Lina something she will not forget: being kind to a scared patient matters just as much as good doctor skills. Lina smiles. She is sure now that she wants to be a doctor more than ever.

versions.title: The Young Doctor's First Case
versions.text:
Lina had dreamed of becoming a doctor for a long time. Her aunt, Dr. Huda, already worked as a doctor. She worked at a small neighborhood clinic. She treated whole families, from tiny babies to old grandparents.

One Saturday, Aunt Huda let Lina come to the clinic. Lina got to shadow her for the whole day, following her from room to room. Lina could hardly wait. She promised to stay quiet and careful.

Soon after the clinic opened, a boy named Omar came in with his worried mother. Omar had fallen off his bike on the way to school. His ankle had swollen up and hurt badly. He was the first patient of the morning. He looked nervous and close to tears.

Aunt Huda knelt down. She began to gently examine the hurt ankle, checking for anything wrong. While she worked, Lina sat beside Omar and spoke to him in a soft, warm voice. She told him a funny story about the time she fell off her own bike, hoping it would give him some comfort.

Slowly, Omar's tears stopped. He felt less nervous now that someone was talking kindly to him. He let Aunt Huda finish her exam without pulling away. She wrapped a soft bandage around his ankle. She told his mother to let him rest and use ice twice a day.

Before they left, Omar smiled. He thanked Lina for helping him feel brave enough to sit still.

That evening, Aunt Huda told Lina something she would remember: comforting a nervous patient matters just as much as strong doctor skills. Lina smiled, sure now that she wanted to become a doctor herself.

Lina had dreamed of becoming a doctor for a long time. She was small enough once to carry a toy stethoscope around the house. Her aunt, Dr. Huda, already worked as a doctor at a small neighborhood clinic. She treated whole families, from tiny babies to old grandparents, every single week.

One Saturday, Aunt Huda let Lina come to the clinic. Lina got to shadow her for the whole day, watching how she cared for each patient. Lina could hardly wait. She promised to stay quiet and careful no matter what happened.

Soon after the clinic opened, a boy named Omar came in with his worried mother. Omar had fallen off his bike on the way to school. His ankle had swollen up and hurt badly overnight. He was the first patient of the morning. He looked nervous, close to tears, and did not want anyone to touch his foot.

Aunt Huda knelt down calmly. She began to examine the hurt ankle, checking gently for anything wrong beneath the swelling. While she worked, Lina sat beside Omar and spoke to him in a warm, soft voice. She told him a funny story about the time she fell off her own bike, hoping the story might offer him some comfort.

Slowly, Omar's tears stopped falling. He felt less nervous now that someone was talking so kindly to him. He let Aunt Huda finish her careful exam without pulling away. She wrapped a soft bandage around his ankle. She told his mother to let him rest and use ice twice a day.

Before they left, Omar smiled brightly. He thanked Lina for helping him feel brave enough to sit still.

That evening, Aunt Huda told Lina something she would always remember: comforting a nervous patient matters just as much as strong doctor skills. Lina smiled, more sure than ever that she wanted to become a doctor herself one day.

versions.title: The Young Doctor's First Case
versions.text:
Lina had dreamed of becoming a doctor for a long time, ever since she was small enough to carry a toy stethoscope around the house and check her stuffed animals' heartbeats. Her aunt, Dr. Huda, already worked as a doctor at a small neighborhood clinic, treating whole families, from tiny babies to old grandparents, nearly every week of the year, sometimes seeing more than twenty patients in a single day.

One Saturday, Aunt Huda let Lina come to the clinic and shadow her for the whole day, following her quietly from room to room and watching how she cared for each patient who walked through the door. Lina could hardly wait, and she promised to stay quiet and careful no matter what happened during the busy day ahead.

Soon after the clinic opened its doors, a boy named Omar came in with his worried mother. Omar had fallen off his bike on the way to school that morning, and his ankle had swollen up and hurt badly overnight. He was the very first patient of the day, and he looked nervous, close to tears, and did not want anyone to touch his sore foot.

Aunt Huda knelt down calmly and began to examine the hurt ankle, checking gently for anything wrong beneath the swelling. While she worked, Lina sat beside Omar and spoke to him in a warm, soft voice, telling him a funny story about the time she fell off her own bike years earlier, hoping the story might offer him some comfort and take his mind off the pain.

Slowly, Omar's tears stopped falling. Feeling far less nervous now that someone was talking so kindly to him, he finally let Aunt Huda finish her careful exam without pulling away in fear. She wrapped a soft bandage around his ankle and told his mother to let him rest and use ice twice a day for a few days.

Before they left, Omar smiled brightly and thanked Lina for helping him feel brave enough to sit still through the whole visit.

That evening, Aunt Huda told Lina something she would always remember: comforting a nervous patient matters just as much as having strong doctor skills, and often matters even more. Lina smiled, more sure than ever that she wanted to become a doctor herself one day, just like her aunt.

versions.title: The Young Doctor's First Case
versions.text:
Lina had dreamed of becoming a doctor for a long time, ever since she was small enough to carry a toy stethoscope around and pretend to check her stuffed animals' heartbeats. Her aunt, Dr. Huda, already worked as a family physician at a small neighborhood clinic, where she treated whole families, from newborn babies to elderly grandparents, nearly every week of the year.

One Saturday, Aunt Huda offered to let Lina shadow her at the clinic for the whole day, following her quietly from room to room and watching, with real interest, how she cared for each patient who walked through the door. Lina could hardly contain her excitement, and she promised to stay quiet and careful, no matter how busy the day became.

Soon after the clinic opened its doors, a boy named Omar arrived with his worried mother. Omar had fallen off his bike on the way to school that morning, and his ankle had swollen up and hurt badly overnight. He was the very first patient of the day, and he looked nervous, close to tears, and did not want anyone near his sore foot.

Aunt Huda knelt down calmly and began the exam procedure, checking gently for anything wrong beneath the swelling while speaking to Omar in a low, steady voice. While she worked, Lina sat beside Omar and tried her best to reassure him, speaking in a warm, soft tone and telling him a funny story about the time she fell off her own bike, hoping it might take his mind off his fear.

Slowly, Omar's tears stopped falling. Feeling far less afraid now that someone was treating him with such empathy, he finally let Aunt Huda finish her careful exam without pulling away. She wrapped a soft bandage around his ankle and told his mother to let him rest and use ice twice a day for the next few days.

Before they left, Omar smiled brightly and thanked Lina for helping him feel brave enough to sit still through the whole visit.

That evening, Aunt Huda told Lina something she would always remember: treating a frightened patient with real compassion matters just as much as having strong medical skill. Lina smiled, more certain than ever that she wanted to become a physician herself one day, just like her aunt.

versions.title: The Young Doctor's First Case
versions.text:
Lina had dreamed of becoming a doctor for a long time, ever since she was small enough to carry a toy stethoscope around and pretend to check her stuffed animals' heartbeats for signs of illness. Her aunt, Dr. Huda, already worked as a family physician at a small neighborhood clinic, where she treated whole families, from newborn infants to elderly grandparents, nearly every week throughout the year.

One Saturday, Aunt Huda offered to let Lina shadow her at the clinic for the whole day, following her quietly from room to room and watching, with real fascination, how she cared for each patient who walked through the door. Lina could hardly contain her excitement, and she promised to stay quiet and careful throughout, however busy the day became.

Soon after the clinic opened its doors, a boy named Omar arrived with his worried mother. Omar had fallen off his bike on the way to school that morning, and his ankle had swollen up quite painfully overnight. He was the very first patient of the day, and he looked nervous, close to tears, and did not want anyone to come near his sore foot.

Aunt Huda knelt down calmly and began the exam procedure, checking gently for anything wrong beneath the swelling while speaking to Omar in a low, steady, soothing voice. While she worked, Lina sat beside Omar and tried her best to reassure him further, speaking in a warm, gentle tone and telling a funny story about the time she had tumbled off her own bike, hoping the story might distract him from his fear.

Slowly, Omar's tears stopped falling. Feeling much less frightened now that someone was treating him with such real empathy, he finally let Aunt Huda finish her careful exam without flinching or pulling away. She wrapped a soft bandage around his ankle and told his mother to let him rest and use ice twice a day for a few days.

Before leaving, Omar smiled broadly and thanked Lina for helping him feel brave enough to stay still through the whole visit.

That evening, Aunt Huda told Lina something she would carry with her for the rest of her life: treating a frightened patient with real compassion matters just as much as having strong medical skill. Lina smiled, more certain than ever that she wanted to become a physician herself, just like her aunt.

versions.title: The Young Doctor's First Case
versions.text:
Lina had dreamed of becoming a doctor for as long as she could remember, ever since she was small enough to carry around a toy stethoscope and solemnly pretend to examine her stuffed animals for supposed signs of illness. Her aunt, Dr. Huda, already worked as a respected family physician at a modest neighborhood clinic, where she treated entire families, from newborn infants to elderly grandparents, nearly every week throughout the year, often without a single day of rest.

One Saturday morning, Aunt Huda offered to let Lina shadow her at the clinic for an entire day, following her quietly from room to room and observing, with evident fascination, precisely how she interacted with each apprehensive patient who walked through the door. Lina could scarcely contain her excitement, and she promised to remain unobtrusive and careful throughout, however hectic the day eventually became.

Soon after the clinic opened its doors, a boy named Omar arrived accompanied by his visibly worried mother. Omar had fallen from his bicycle on the way to school that morning, and his ankle had swollen up quite painfully overnight. He was the very first patient of the day, and his anxious demeanor made it obvious that he was nervous, close to tears, and entirely unwilling to let anyone approach his sore foot.

Aunt Huda knelt down calmly and began the examination procedure, checking gently for anything seriously wrong beneath the swelling while speaking to Omar in a low, steady, reassuring voice that seemed to calm him slightly. While she worked, Lina sat down beside Omar and tried her best to reassure him further, speaking in a warm, gentle tone and recounting a humorous little story about the time she herself had tumbled off her own bicycle years earlier, hoping the memory might distract him sufficiently from his fear.

Gradually, Omar's tears stopped falling altogether. Feeling considerably less frightened now that someone was treating him with such evident empathy, he finally allowed Aunt Huda to complete her careful examination without flinching or attempting to pull away. She wrapped a soft bandage securely around his ankle and instructed his mother to let him rest completely and apply ice twice daily for the following several days.

Before departing, Omar smiled broadly and thanked Lina sincerely for helping him summon the courage to remain still throughout the entire uncomfortable visit.

That evening, Aunt Huda shared something with Lina that she would carry with her for the rest of her life: treating a frightened patient with genuine compassion matters every bit as much as possessing exceptional medical skill, perhaps even more. Lina smiled contentedly, more certain than ever that she someday wanted to become a physician herself, just like her remarkable and deeply admirable aunt.

versions.title: The Young Doctor's First Case
versions.text:
Lina had dreamed of becoming a doctor for as long as she could remember, carrying around a toy stethoscope as a small child and solemnly examining her stuffed animals for imaginary signs of illness. Her aunt, Dr. Huda, already worked as a respected family physician at a modest neighborhood clinic, treating entire families, from newborn infants to elderly grandparents, nearly every week of the year, often without a single day of rest, and when Aunt Huda offered to let Lina shadow her for an entire Saturday, following her quietly from room to room and observing exactly how she interacted with each apprehensive patient, Lina could scarcely contain her excitement.

Soon after the clinic opened that morning, a boy named Omar arrived with his visibly worried mother, having fallen from his bicycle on the way to school and swollen his ankle painfully overnight. As the very first patient of the day, his anxious demeanor made it immediately obvious that he was nervous, close to tears, and entirely unwilling to let anyone approach his sore foot. Aunt Huda knelt down calmly and began the examination procedure, checking gently beneath the swelling while speaking to Omar in a low, steady, reassuring voice, and while she worked, Lina sat beside Omar trying her best to reassure him further, recounting a humorous story about once tumbling off her own bicycle, hoping the memory might distract him sufficiently from his fear.

Gradually, Omar's tears stopped falling altogether, and feeling considerably less frightened now that someone was treating him with such profound empathy, he finally allowed Aunt Huda to complete her careful examination without flinching. She wrapped a soft bandage securely around his ankle, instructed his mother to let him rest and apply ice twice daily, and before departing, Omar smiled broadly and thanked Lina sincerely for helping him summon the courage to remain still throughout the entire uncomfortable visit.

That evening, Aunt Huda shared something with Lina that she would undoubtedly carry with her for the rest of her life: treating a frightened patient with genuine compassion matters every bit as much as possessing exceptional medical skill, and arguably matters even more, since a frightened child who cannot hold still can make even the most routine procedure far more difficult than it needs to be. versions.title: The Young Doctor's First Case
versions.text:
Lina had dreamed of becoming a doctor for as long as she could remember, carrying around a toy stethoscope as a small child and solemnly examining her stuffed animals for imaginary, invented signs of illness. Her aunt, Dr. Huda, already worked as a respected family physician at a modest neighborhood clinic, treating entire families, from newborn infants to elderly grandparents, nearly every week of the year, often without a single day of rest, and when Aunt Huda offered to let Lina shadow her for an entire Saturday, following her quietly from room to room and observing precisely how she interacted with each apprehensive patient, Lina could scarcely contain her overwhelming excitement.

Soon after the clinic opened its doors that morning, a boy named Omar arrived with his visibly worried mother, having fallen from his bicycle on the way to school and swollen his ankle painfully overnight. As the very first patient of the day, his anxious demeanor made it immediately obvious that he was nervous, close to tears, and entirely unwilling to let anyone approach his tender, sore foot. Aunt Huda knelt down calmly and began the examination procedure, checking gently beneath the swelling while speaking to Omar in a low, steady, reassuring voice, and while she worked, Lina sat beside Omar trying her utmost to reassure him further, recounting a humorous anecdote about once tumbling off her own bicycle, hoping the memory might sufficiently distract him from his evident fear.

Gradually, Omar's tears stopped falling altogether, and feeling considerably less frightened now that someone was treating him with such profound empathy, he finally allowed Aunt Huda to complete her meticulous examination without flinching or attempting to withdraw. She wrapped a soft bandage securely around his ankle, instructed his mother to let him rest completely and apply ice twice daily for several subsequent days, and before departing, Omar smiled broadly and thanked Lina sincerely for helping him summon the courage required to remain still throughout the entire uncomfortable visit.

That evening, Aunt Huda shared something with Lina that she would undoubtedly carry with her for the remainder of her life: treating a frightened patient with genuine compassion matters every bit as much as possessing exceptional medical skill, and arguably matters even more, since a frightened child who cannot hold still can transform even the most routine procedure into something considerably more difficult than it otherwise needs to be. Lina smiled contentedly, more certain than ever that she someday wanted to become a physician herself, recognizing, perhaps for the first time with complete clarity, that the finest doctors are ultimately remembered not merely for their accurate diagnoses but for the simple, profoundly human comfort they manage to offer at a patient's most vulnerable and frightening moment.

keyWords.definition: a person trained to treat sick or hurt people
keyWords.example: My uncle is a doctor at the big hospital downtown.

keyWords.definition: a person who is being cared for by a doctor
keyWords.example: The nurse brought the patient a glass of cold water.

keyWords.definition: caring and gentle toward other people
keyWords.example: It was kind of her to share her lunch with a new student.
The little puppy was scared of the loud thunder.

keyWords.definition: paying close attention so as not to make a mistake or cause harm
keyWords.example: Be careful when you carry the hot pot to the table.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A girl who shadows her doctor aunt and learns that kindness matters as much as skill
A boy who spends his whole summer learning how to ride his new bicycle safely
A doctor who spends the entire day searching for her missing medical tools
A girl who feels much too afraid to ever visit the busy neighborhood clinic
questions.why: The story follows Lina as she watches her aunt treat Omar and learns that kindness is as important as medical skill.

wrong.B: The story is not about teaching bike safety.
wrong.C: Aunt Huda never loses any tools in the story.
wrong.D: Lina is not afraid of the clinic; Omar is the one who is scared.

questions.stem: How does Omar hurt his ankle?
options: He trips over a small rug while running at home
He falls off his bicycle on the way to school
He falls down the stairs inside the busy clinic
He twists it while playing soccer after school
questions.why: The story says Omar fell off his bicycle on the way to school and hurt his ankle.

wrong.A: The story does not mention a rug or his home.
wrong.C: The story does not say he fell at the clinic.
wrong.D: The story does not mention soccer.

questions.stem: What does Aunt Huda do when Omar arrives?
options: She sends him straight home
She calls his teacher on the phone
She carefully examines his hurt ankle
She gives him a toy stethoscope to hold
questions.why: In the story, Aunt Huda looks at the sore ankle very carefully.

wrong.A: She treats Omar instead of sending him home.
wrong.B: The story does not mention calling his teacher.
wrong.D: The toy stethoscope belongs to Lina, not Omar, and is not in this scene.

questions.stem: Why does Omar stop crying?
options: Because his mother leaves the room for a few minutes
Because the pain suddenly disappears from his arm and hand
Because Aunt Huda gives him some candy to eat after the visit
Because Lina sits with him and tells him a kind, funny story
questions.why: The story says Omar stops crying and feels safe after Lina talks to him kindly and tells a funny story.

wrong.A: His mother stays in the room during the visit.
wrong.B: The story does not say the pain disappears.
wrong.C: The story does not mention candy.

questions.stem: How does Lina likely feel about becoming a doctor by the end of the story?
options: She feels even more excited to become one
She decides she would rather be a teacher
She feels unsure about her dream now
She feels scared of helping patients
questions.why: After hearing her aunt's lesson about kindness, Lina smiles and wants to be a doctor even more than before.

wrong.B: Nothing in the story suggests she wants to be a teacher.
wrong.C: She feels more certain, not less certain.
wrong.D: She comforts Omar calmly; she is not scared of patients.

questions.stem: Why is Omar probably so scared when he first arrives?
options: He does not like his mother and wants to go home
He is afraid of Lina and what she will say to him
He is hurt and does not know what will happen next
He does not want to go to school that day
questions.why: Omar just fell and hurt his ankle, and being hurt and unsure of what the doctor will do can make a child feel scared.

wrong.A: His mother brings him in to help him; nothing suggests he dislikes her.
wrong.B: Lina is the one who helps him feel calm, not someone he fears.
wrong.D: The story is about his injury, not about school.

questions.stem: In the story, a patient is —
options: a doctor's helper who works in a clinic
a person who is being cared for by a doctor
a kind of medicine that a doctor gives to sick people
a type of bandage that covers a cut or a wound
questions.why: Omar is called the patient because he is the person Aunt Huda examines and treats.

wrong.A: Lina helps, but she is not the patient.
wrong.C: A patient is a person, not medicine.
wrong.D: A patient is not a bandage.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the story with what Aunt Huda tells Lina?
options: To explain how clinics are built by workers and nurses in a town
To describe what Omar eats for lunch each day with his family
To show that medicine is too hard to learn for most young people
To teach the lesson that kindness matters as much as medical skill
questions.why: Aunt Huda's final words sum up the main lesson of the story for Lina and for readers.

wrong.A: The story never describes how clinics are built.
wrong.B: Omar's lunch is never mentioned.
wrong.C: The ending encourages Lina, rather than saying medicine is too hard.

LOW.prompt: Would you rather be like Aunt Huda or like Lina in this story? Explain your choice using at least two details from the story.
checklist: I clearly said which person I would rather be like.
I used at least two details from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I would rather be like Lina. She sits with Omar and tells him a funny story so he feels brave. I would like to help scared patients feel better that way. Aunt Huda's job is important too, but talking kindly to someone seems like something I could do right now.

keyWords.definition: to look at something closely to check it
keyWords.example: The teacher examined my drawing before hanging it up.

keyWords.definition: to help someone feel calmer or less upset
keyWords.example: She tried to comfort her little brother after he fell down.

keyWords.definition: a small place where doctors treat people who are not very sick
keyWords.example: We walked to the clinic to get my sister's cough checked.

keyWords.definition: to follow and watch someone closely to learn what they do
keyWords.example: The new worker got to shadow an older worker for a week.

keyWords.definition: worried or uneasy about something that is about to happen
keyWords.example: I felt nervous before my first swimming lesson.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?

Aunt Huda runs the busiest clinic in the city, and she has more patients than any doctor
Omar does not want to ride his bicycle again after he falls and hurts his ankle
Lina decides medicine is too difficult for her and chooses a different job when she grows up
questions.why: The story builds toward Aunt Huda's lesson that comforting a nervous patient matters as much as medical skill.

wrong.B: The story never compares clinics or calls it the busiest.
wrong.C: The story never says Omar gives up his bicycle.
wrong.D: The ending shows Lina feeling more certain about medicine, not less.

questions.stem: What is Lina doing at the clinic for the day?
options: Cleaning and tidying the entire waiting room
Shadowing her aunt and watching how she treats patients
Answering phone calls for the busy clinic all day in the clinic
Selling bandages and medicine to patients
questions.why: Aunt Huda invites Lina to shadow her, following her from room to room all day.

wrong.A: The story never mentions Lina cleaning.
wrong.C: The story never mentions phone calls.

MID.prompt: Explain why Aunt Huda says that comforting a nervous patient matters as much as having good doctor skills. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained Aunt Huda's lesson in my own words.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Aunt Huda says this because kindness helped Omar just as much as medicine did. When Omar was nervous and crying, Lina comforted him with a soft voice and a funny story, and he calmed down enough to let Aunt Huda finish examining him. If Omar had stayed scared, the examination would have been much harder. This shows that a patient's feelings matter just as much as a doctor's skill.

keyWords.definition: a doctor, especially one who treats general illnesses rather than performing surgery
keyWords.example: The physician listened carefully to the old man's heartbeat.

keyWords.definition: to say or do something that removes someone's fear or doubt
keyWords.example: The pilot reassured the passengers during the bumpy flight.

keyWords.definition: the ability to understand and share another person's feelings
keyWords.example: Good nurses show empathy toward frightened patients.

keyWords.definition: a series of actions done in a certain order to complete a medical or other task
keyWords.example: The dentist explained the procedure before cleaning my teeth.

keyWords.definition: a strong feeling of sympathy that makes someone want to help another person
keyWords.example: The firefighters showed great compassion toward the frightened family.

HIGH.prompt: Do you agree that compassion matters as much as medical skill when treating a frightened patient? Support your answer with evidence from the story.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the question.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that compassion matters as much as medical skill when treating a frightened patient. In the story, Omar is too scared to let Aunt Huda examine him properly until Lina comforts him with a warm voice and a funny story. Without that compassion, the careful examination procedure might have taken much longer or upset Omar even more. Someone might argue that medical knowledge is what actually fixes an injury, but even perfect skill is hard to use well on a child who will not stay still, so comforting a patient is often what makes good treatment possible in the first place.
